title: Data Models
summary: The shape you impose on data decides which questions are cheap and which are painful. A tour from trees to tables to JSON — why relational won, and when the others beat it.

blocks.markdown:
A **data model** is the shape you impose on data — the rules for how facts are structured, linked, and queried. Choose the wrong shape and simple questions turn expensive; choose the right one and they fall out almost for free.

- It fixes three things: **structures** (tables, trees, documents, graphs), **operations** (how you read and write), and **constraints** (what must always stay true).
- The model decides which questions are cheap and which are painful — it is the single biggest data-design decision you make.
- Databases are classified by the model they implement: relational, document, graph, key-value.
- **Relational** (tables linked by values) won the bulk of the market; the others exist because a few problem shapes fit them far better.

This topic is the map of the territory; the rest of the track drills into each model in depth.

blocks.subTitle: The families at a glance
blocks.markdown:
The model families you'll meet, by the shape they store and what they're best at.

| Model | Shape | Best at |
|---|---|---|
| Relational | Tables of rows | Joins, correctness |
| Document | Nested JSON | Flexible records |
| Graph | Nodes + edges | Relationship walks |
| Key-value | Key to blob | Fast lookups |

Most real systems combine two or three of these rather than betting everything on one.

blocks.subTitle: Hierarchical
blocks.markdown:
The **hierarchical model** stores data as one big tree: every record has exactly **one parent**, and you read by walking down from the root. It mirrors how 1960s storage worked — tape and early disk were sequential, so a fixed top-down path was fast and natural.

- **Great at one-to-many.** A department owning many employees, a folder holding many files — parent-to-child reads are a single walk down the tree.
- **Bad at many-to-many.** Model a student enrolled in many courses, each course holding many students, and you must **duplicate** the course under every student — or invent fake links. Updates then drift out of sync.
- **Rigid access path.** The tree *is* the query plan; a question the hierarchy didn't anticipate means restructuring the data or scanning the whole thing.

**Real system:** IBM's **IMS** (1966, built for the Apollo program) is the classic hierarchical DBMS — and it still processes core transactions at large banks today. This rigidity is exactly the pain the relational model set out to fix.

blocks.subTitle: Network
blocks.markdown:
The **network model** (the CODASYL standard, early 1970s) generalized the tree: a record can have **many parents**, wired together by explicit **pointers**.

- **It fixed many-to-many.** A student could link directly to many courses and a course to many students — no duplication, unlike the hierarchy.
- **But you navigated by hand.** A query meant chasing pointer chains in code: *from this student, follow the enrolled-in link to each course*. Powerful, but every question was a mini graph-walk you wrote yourself.
- **Access paths were baked in.** The links you defined up front *were* your query options; a new kind of question often meant redesigning the pointer structure and rewriting programs.

It was faster than hierarchy for complex data, but that manual navigation is precisely what the relational model set out to abolish.

blocks.subTitle: Relational — the winner
blocks.markdown:
The **relational model** (Edgar Codd, 1970) made a radical bet: **throw out pointers entirely**. Data is just **tables of rows**, and relationships are expressed by **matching values** (keys), never by stored links.

- **Declarative, not navigational.** You state *what* you want in SQL ("the orders of customers in Delhi"); the engine's optimizer decides *how* to fetch it. No hand-written traversal.
- **Any join, any time.** Because links are just values, you can join any two tables on the fly — even relationships nobody planned for at design time.
- **Backed by math.** It rests on set theory and relational algebra, which is why queries are so predictable and optimizable → [relational-model-keys](relational-model-keys).

That clean separation of *what* from *how* is why relational databases have dominated for over 50 years, outlasting every 'relational is dead' prediction.

blocks.subTitle: The timeline
blocks.markdown:
Each model was born to fix the previous one's biggest pain.

- **Hierarchy → Network:** break the one-parent limit to allow many-to-many.
- **Network → Relational:** stop hand-navigating pointers; query by value instead.
- **Relational → Object:** map richer program objects into storage.
- **Relational → NoSQL:** relax guarantees to scale horizontally and store flexible shapes.

Notice the shape of it: relational didn't get replaced — it stayed the center, and newer models grew around it for specific needs.

blocks.subTitle: ER: a design model, not a storage one
blocks.markdown:
The **ER (entity-relationship) model** is the odd one out: it's not how data is *stored*, it's how you *design* it before any table exists.

- You sketch **entities** (the nouns: Customer, Order, Product), their **attributes** (a Customer has a name and email), and the **relationships** between them (a Customer *places* an Order).
- It's deliberately implementation-free — a whiteboard language for agreeing on a design with teammates and non-engineers.
- You then mechanically **convert** the diagram into relational tables: entities become tables, relationships become foreign keys or join tables.

Think of ER as the architect's blueprint and the relational schema as the built house. Full treatment in [er-model](er-model).

blocks.subTitle: Object & semi-structured
blocks.markdown:
Two more families round out the picture:

- **Object / object-relational.** Store data as **objects** with types and inheritance, so it maps cleanly to OOP code without an ORM translating back and forth. Pure object databases stayed niche, but relational engines absorbed the good parts — Postgres has composite types, arrays, and even table inheritance.
- **Semi-structured.** Records are **self-describing** — each carries its own field names, usually as **JSON or XML** — so two rows in the same collection can have different fields. This is the backbone of document databases and shines when the shape is fluid or varies per record.

The trade is explicit: semi-structured drops the rigid, engine-enforced schema in exchange for flexibility, and pushes the job of keeping data consistent into your application → [nosql-modern-databases](nosql-modern-databases).

Choose the model by the question you'll ask most, not by what's trendy.

- **Complex queries, joins, multi-row correctness** → **relational**. Orders, payments, inventory — anything where a half-finished write is unacceptable.
- **Flexible, evolving, deeply nested records** → **document**. Product catalogs, user profiles, CMS content where every item differs.
- **Relationships *are* the data** (friends-of-friends, fraud rings, dependencies) → **graph**. Traversals that would be dozens of SQL joins collapse into one query.
- **Dead-simple, ultra-fast key lookups** → **key-value**. Sessions, feature flags, caches.

Default to relational — it's the most general and the easiest to hire for. Switch only when the data's natural shape genuinely fights the tables, and even then often just for *part* of the system.

What teams actually run in production today:

- **Relational** — **PostgreSQL** and **MySQL** are the default for business-critical data; Postgres is the common "just use this" answer.
- **Document** — **MongoDB** for fast-moving app data and prototypes where the schema keeps changing.
- **Graph** — **Neo4j** for social graphs, recommendations, and fraud detection.
- **Key-value** — **Redis** for caching, sessions, and rate limiters.
- **Multi-model** — increasingly one engine does several jobs: Postgres with **JSONB** gives you relational tables *and* schemaless documents in the same database.

The modern default isn't "pick one model forever" — it's relational as the backbone, with a document column or a cache bolted on where each earns its place.

The misconceptions that cause real damage:

- **"NoSQL replaced relational."** It didn't. NoSQL added shapes for scale and flexibility; relational still runs banking, commerce, and most systems of record on earth.
- **"Schema-less means no design."** Document data absolutely still needs a modeled shape — you've just moved enforcement from the database into application code, where bugs are easier to introduce.
- **"An ER diagram is the database."** It's the *design*; you still have to map it to real tables and constraints.
- **"Pick one model for everything."** Forcing graph-shaped or document-shaped data into rigid tables (or the reverse) is a classic source of pain.

The meta-mistake: choosing a model for its buzz instead of for the questions you actually need to answer.

blocks.subTitle: SQL vs NoSQL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: SQL vs NoSQL — when would you choose each?**

Reach for **SQL / relational** when you need multi-row correctness (ACID), rich ad-hoc queries, and joins — orders, payments, anything that must reconcile. Reach for **NoSQL** when you need to scale writes horizontally, store flexible or evolving shapes, or serve one dominant access pattern very fast.

Concretely: a payments ledger → Postgres; a product catalog with wildly varying attributes → a document store; a session cache → Redis.

The senior signal is **refusing the false binary**: most real systems use relational as the backbone plus a document field or cache where it earns its place. The deciding factors are consistency needs, query shape, and scale — not novelty.

blocks.subTitle: Database vs DBMS vs data model
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a database, a DBMS, and a data model?**

**Data** is raw facts. A **database** is data organized for a purpose. A **DBMS** is the software that stores, protects, and serves that database (MySQL, Postgres). A **data model** is the abstract shape the DBMS imposes — relational, document, graph.

So: the relational *model* is the idea of tables-linked-by-values; **PostgreSQL** is a *DBMS* implementing it; the tables of your app are the *database*; the rows inside are the *data*.

Mixing these up — e.g. saying "SQL is a database" — is a common junior tell.

blocks.subTitle: Why relational won
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why did the relational model beat the hierarchical and network models?**

Both older models forced you to **navigate** data along pre-defined pointer paths, so any unanticipated query meant redesigning structures and rewriting code. Codd's relational model replaced physical links with **values (keys)** and gave you a **declarative** language (SQL): you say *what* you want, the optimizer decides *how*.

That killed the rigidity — any table joins any other on the fly — and the underlying relational algebra made queries provably optimizable. Flexibility plus a solid mathematical footing is why it has dominated for 50 years.

blocks.subTitle: When a graph beats relational
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Give an example where a graph database clearly beats relational.**

**Friends-of-friends-of-friends** — or fraud-ring detection, or dependency resolution. In SQL each "hop" is another self-join; going four or five levels deep means four or five joins over an exploding intermediate set, and it gets slow and unreadable.

A graph database stores explicit edges and walks them directly, so a variable-depth traversal is one natural query that stays fast as depth grows.

Rule of thumb: when the **relationships themselves are the primary thing you query** — not just an occasional join — reach for a graph.

blocks.subTitle: Is document data really schema-less?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Is a schema-less (document) database really schema-less?**

No — it's **schema-*flexible*, not schema-free**. The engine won't enforce a fixed set of columns, but your data still has an implicit shape that your application depends on.

You've simply moved schema enforcement from the database into app code (and often a validation library). That buys flexibility for evolving data, but the responsibility for consistency — and the bugs when two code paths write different shapes — now lives with you.

Saying "no schema needed" is the trap; the schema didn't vanish, it just stopped being enforced for you.
